title: Entrelac crochet
subtitle: How to build the interlocking diagonal square structure of entrelac
excerpt: Entrelac crochet builds fabric from a diagonal grid of small interlocked squares. Each square is worked in a different orientation from its neighbour and picks up stitches from the side of the adjacent square rather than a foundation chain. The resulting fabric looks woven and textural without being woven at all. It is worked entirely in rows of small squares, each crocheted directly onto the last.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing). Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: The individual block unit of entrelac crochet. Each square is worked by picking up stitches along the side of an adjacent square and turning the work to build the square row by row. The squares interlock without seaming.
The half-square triangles worked at the beginning and end of an entrelac row to create a straight edge. Base triangles are increased one stitch per row on one side.

content.text: lock together by picking up stitches from the edges of already-worked squares rather than requiring seaming. The fabric looks woven but is built by turning the work and working back and forth within each small square. Each square uses the side stitches of the adjacent square as its foundation row. The direction of work rotates 90 degrees from one square to the next, which gives entrelac fabric its characteristic criss-cross texture.

items.name: Yarn in one or two colours
items.note: Entrelac shows most clearly in a solid colour. Two alternating colours emphasise the diagonal grid.

items.name: Stitch markers
items.note: Mark the corner of each square as you work to make stitch pickup easier.

content.text: Working the first row of base triangles

Make a foundation chain slightly longer than the intended finished width (for a 4-square-wide piece, chain approximately 20 plus turning chains). The exact count depends on the square size used in the pattern.

by working into the foundation chain, adding one more stitch per row until the triangle reaches the full square width. Turn at the end of each row. When the triangle is the full square width, it forms the left-hand triangle at the edge of the first row.
Work the next base triangle directly beside the first, picking up from the foundation chain. Continue until the full width has base triangles all across.
Working the first row of squares

At the top of the base triangles, work the first full square: pick up one stitch for each row of the base triangle along its side edge, then turn and work back. Continue turning and working back across the same stitch count for as many rows as the square has stitches across. This builds one full square sitting at 90 degrees to the base triangle.

At the end of the square, pick up stitches along the edge of the next base triangle to start the next square. Each square is thus joined to its neighbour during construction: no seaming needed after the fact.

items.symptom: The squares are not the same size across the row
items.cause: The number of stitches picked up along the side of each base triangle varied.
items.fix: Pick up exactly one stitch per row of the base triangle (no more, no less). Mark the top and bottom of each triangle side with a stitch marker to make the boundary clear.

items.symptom: The interlocked squares are not lying flat (the fabric is ruffling)
items.cause: Too many stitches are being picked up along the edges, adding extra width.
items.fix: Count the stitches per square after picking up the side stitches. It should match the number of rows in the previous square exactly. Remove and redo the pickup row if the count is off.

items.symptom: The direction of the grain in the squares looks random rather than diagonal
items.cause: The work was not turned consistently between squares.
items.fix: Each full square must be worked by turning the work and going back and forth within the square's stitch count. The 90-degree grain rotation happens automatically when each square picks up from the side of the previous one.

content.text: Begin with a 2-by-2-square sampler: 2 base triangles, then 2 full squares, then 2 closing triangles at the top. Keeping the sample small lets you understand the pickup-stitch logic without managing a large piece. Once the pickup technique is comfortable, the full fabric scales up naturally by adding more base triangles per row.
